content:
I was looking into creating bundled structures Antichain and MaxAntichain analogous to UpperSet and LowerSet. However, it turns out the definitions of IsUpperSet and IsLowerSet use [LE α], while IsAntichain explicitly takes a relation.

This seems strange to me. Is there a good reason for this difference? If not, does anyone have insight into which version is preferable? If the reason is so IsAntichain can also be used for independent sets, would it make sense to create a specialization for LE?

I would love a version of IsUpperSet and friends that take a relation (although strangely, the name docs#IsRelUpperSet is taken).
Types don't always have a sensible LE, but it can still be useful to talk about something wrt a relation.

I like the solution of allowing arbitrary relations, and adding abbrevs for LE and friends.
See e.g. docs#IsWellFounded / docs#WellFoundedLT / docs#WellFoundedGT which I think work pretty well.
Also docs#IsMulCommutative / docs#IsAddCommutative / docs#OrderEmbedding / docs#OrderIso
There was also talk about doing the same with docs#Ordinal.IsPrincipal
cc @Violeta Hernández, and perhaps @Vlad Tsyrklevich as the author of Dilworth's theorem
do we ever use these for other relations
Oh about the bundled structures, I think LE (or LT?) is probably best. The Is* predicate versions are good enough for the other cases.

Aaron Liu said:

do we ever use these for other relations

Yes, WellFounded/RelHom/RelEmbedding/RelIso are often used with other relations, and for chains/antichains see e.g. docs#SimpleGraph.isClique_iff_isChain_adj and docs#SimpleGraph.isIndepSet_iff_isAntichain_adj

Also for lower sets, see e.g. docs#InitialSeg which spells IsLowerSet manually because there's no general version, and so loses out on its API
do we use that one with any other relations
I am :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

Aaron Liu said:

do we use that one with any other relations

We do, in order to define ordinals. I really wish we didn’t.

I’m generally of the idea that we win little and lose a lot by generalizing these sorts of notions to bare relations. Given a bare relation (even one that might be totally or even well ordered), it’s awkward to write the corresponding < relation, we can’t easily write infima/minimums or suprema/maximums, and we lose out on the many theorems we’ve already proved for the order typeclasses. Also, to_dual stops working.

Aaron Liu said:

can we not do that then

In my ideal world, docs#IsWellOrder would be gone entirely, and replaced with docs#LinearOrder + docs#WellFoundedLT or docs#WellFoundedGT. The issue is that we do often make use of unbundled well-orders, as inconvenient as they are (e.g. when we well-order the reals). My idea for a while has been to make a WellOrder type alias endowing a type with a well-order (perhaps even one of minimum order type), but I haven’t gotten around to this.
Didn't you want to define Ordinals as a Subtype of OrderType?

At minimum, these should all be consistent, right? Also, wouldn't talking about multiple relations on the same type become needlessly difficult without generalized versions? It seems like it should be relatively straightforward to prove general results for LE specializations first, making use of the order typeclass theorems, and then lift them to generalized versions.

The following discussion seems relevant too
#mathlib4 > Infinite Ramsey theory @ 💬
It seems to me that results that do not necessitate transitivity or antisymmetry should be available as such.
If we do generalize these to other relations, am I correct in assuming the generalized versions should not be included in to_dual?
